_comment: GROUND TRUTH for calibration's mechanical detection. /pitlane-setup does not carry this
knowledge in its prose and nothing else carries a second copy — it defers
here, because one table restated in three places is a doc-rot generator. hooks/scripts/detect.sh
reads this file; the skill narrates what detect.sh returns.
HOOKS DO NOT DETECT FROM THIS FILE. Detection happens once, at calibrate time, with a human
present. By the time a hook runs, every answer derived from here is already in the
target repo's committed .claude/worktree-profile.json.
ONE HOOK-TIME READER EXISTS, in bootstrap: wt_report_drift() in bootstrap-lib.sh reads the
detectionVersion, each rule's markers and dir, and the shell markers, purely to COMPARE them
against the profile's evidence block and against which files exist. String compares and file
tests only -- it never chooses a strategy, an install command or a shell, which is what would
make it detection. It costs one interpreter start on the session-start path, and only for a
profile that carries an evidence block to compare.
To add an ecosystem: add an entry to `deps`. That is the whole change — no edit to detect.sh,
no edit to the skill.
MATCHING IS FIRST-MATCH-WINS IN ARRAY ORDER, PER MARKER. Each `deps` entry lists the `markers`
that trigger it; the first entry whose marker exists AND whose optional `when` guard holds
claims that marker, and later entries listing the same marker are skipped. That is how the two
yarn rules coexist: the Yarn Berry rule is guarded on .yarnrc.yml and sits BEFORE the classic
one, so a Berry repo takes it and a classic repo falls through. `shells` is ordered by
precedence the same way, ending in a marker:null catch-all so matching always terminates.
FLAT BY DESIGN. An earlier revision nested these guarded rules inside a `variants` array on
their parent entry, which reads well but cannot be consumed: the plugin's JSON layer addresses
values by dotted path and cannot index into an array, so reading an object inside an array
element would have meant a third JSON parser in a codebase whose two existing ones have already
diverged twice. Ordering plus a `when` guard expresses the same thing with no nesting.
`reason` strings are DATA, not decoration. They are what the developer is shown when calibration
proposes a value, so they must state the why in one line a developer can disagree with. Improvised
reasons would differ run to run; these do not.
NO TAB CHARACTERS ANYWHERE IN THIS FILE'S VALUES. detect.sh emits tab-separated records, and it
strips tabs defensively, but a tab here would be a silent field split at the source.
EVERY RULE THAT MANAGES A DIRECTORY CARRIES EITHER A `verify` OR A `noVerify`. A verify runs from the
worktree root in the HOST shell, so it is a plain file test, never a tool call, and it names a file
only a FINISHED install writes -- checked against a real install of each tool, and against a failed
one. bootstrap trusts it over the install's exit code, so a check that also passes on the tree a
failed install leaves behind is worse than none: it turns `failed` into `warn`. Where no such file
exists (bun, mix, poetry, pipenv), the rule says why in `noVerify` instead, detect.sh passes that on
in a depNote, and setup asks the developer for a check. A rule with `requiresDir` names a directory
the tool creates in-project only when configured to; when it is absent, detect.sh withholds the
default (it would fail in every worktree) and setup asks instead. Rules with no `dir` (cargo, go)
keep their dependencies in a machine-wide cache and need neither.
VERSION 3: per-rule verify defaults, and no rule hardlinks a Python venv any more.
_comment_sameDirPolicy: Several markers can resolve to the same `dir` — a repo mid-migration with both pnpm-lock.yaml and
package-lock.json, or both bun.lock and bun.lockb, all claim node_modules. Two profile entries for
one directory is not a cosmetic problem: their strategies conflict (one hardlinks a tree the other
then reinstalls) and bootstrap does the work twice.
So: at most ONE entry per `dir`. Ties are broken by array order — the first matching entry wins —
and calibration must SAY which markers it dropped and why, never drop one silently. A repo with two
live lockfiles for one directory is usually a mistake the developer wants to know about.

deps.reason: composer materialises real bytes per project, so a hardlink copy is near-instant and costs almost no disk

pnpm already content-addresses packages in a global store and hardlinks them in, so the tree is mostly not real disk and sharing it is unsafe — node_modules/.modules.yaml records the project it was installed for
npm materialises real bytes per project, so hardlinking beats reinstalling
Yarn Berry keeps its own zip cache and, under Plug'n'Play, has no node_modules to share at all — so install rather than hardlink, and --frozen-lockfile is the deprecated spelling of --immutable
classic yarn materialises real bytes per project, so hardlinking beats reinstalling

deps.noVerify: bun (1.3) writes no marker file into node_modules, and a failed install keeps the tree it extracted -- a postinstall that exits non-zero leaves every package in place -- so no file test separates a finished install from a broken one; ask for a package this repo always installs, e.g. test -f node_modules/<package>/package.json
deps.reason: bun installs from its own global cache, so a fresh install is cheap and sharing the tree buys nothing. bun.lockb is the pre-1.2 binary lockfile; newer repos use the text bun.lock — one entry covers both, since a repo mid-migration must not get two
uv hardlinks from its own global cache and a sync is seconds — and a venv is never hardlinked anyway: its scripts and editable-install mappings hard-code the main checkout's path
deps.notes: the verify holds because uv creates the venv unseeded (no pip) and links packages only once every one is resolved and downloaded, so a .dist-info appears only when installing began; .venv/bin/python and .venv/.lock exist before resolution, so a failed sync passes a check on them. A virtual project with no dependencies at all writes no .dist-info, and needs a different check.

deps.noVerify: poetry creates the venv -- its interpreter and a seeded pip with its own .dist-info -- before resolving, so every generic file test on the venv also passes after a failed install; ask for a package this repo always installs, e.g. a glob for its .dist-info under the venv's site-packages
deps.reason: a venv is never hardlinked: its scripts, activate files and editable-install mappings hard-code the main checkout's path, so a linked copy installs into and imports from the main checkout
deps.notes: poetry only creates .venv inside the project when virtualenvs.in-project is set; otherwise the venv lives under poetry's own cache and a .venv check would fail in every worktree. `poetry install --sync` was the older spelling and is deprecated in Poetry 2.0 in favour of `poetry sync`; plain `poetry install` is correct on both.

deps.noVerify: pipenv creates the venv -- its interpreter and a seeded pip with its own .dist-info -- before installing, so every generic file test on the venv also passes after a failed install; ask for a package this repo always installs, e.g. a glob for its .dist-info under the venv's site-packages
deps.reason: a venv is never hardlinked: its scripts, activate files and editable-install mappings hard-code the main checkout's path, so a linked copy installs into and imports from the main checkout
deps.notes: pipenv's DEFAULT is a venv outside the project, under ~/.local/share/virtualenvs/<project>-<hash>. .venv is used only when PIPENV_VENV_IN_PROJECT is set or a .venv already exists, so a .venv check would fail in every worktree of a repo that uses the default.

deps.reason: a vendored bundle is real bytes per project, so hardlinking beats reinstalling — but ONLY when bundler is configured to vendor; see requiresDir
deps.notes: vendor/bundle exists only when bundler is configured with a `path` (check .bundle/config). Otherwise gems are installed into the system/rbenv gem home and there is nothing per-project to copy. The verify reads vendor/bundle/ruby, which bundler creates under a configured path; the ruby version directory below it changes with the interpreter, so it is not named.

deps.noVerify: mix deps.get writes one deps/<package>/ per dependency and no marker for the whole fetch, so a fetch that fails part-way leaves a deps/ every generic file test passes; `mix deps.loadpaths --no-compile` does tell (it fails on any missing or out-of-date dependency) but needs elixir, and a verify runs in the host shell -- use it only where elixir is on the host's PATH, else test for a package this repo always fetches
deps.reason: mix fetches real source per project into deps/, so hardlinking beats refetching
crate sources are already shared through CARGO_HOME, and target/ is build output that a stale hardlink actively corrupts for incremental builds — so there is nothing per-project worth copying
deps.notes: dir is null rather than "target" on purpose: `install` is documented as the command that populates `dir`, and `cargo fetch` populates CARGO_HOME, not target/. Nothing here is managed, so naming a directory would be a claim the entry does not honour.

deps.reason: go has no per-project dependency directory at all — GOMODCACHE is already shared between every checkout on the machine, so there is nothing for a worktree to copy

shells.reason: hooks launch from the host shell, where this project's toolchain is not on PATH; a flake means `nix develop` is the way in
a non-flake nix project enters through nix-shell, which takes the command as ONE STRING rather than as argv
direnv already encodes how to enter this project's environment, and `direnv exec .` reproduces it non-interactively

shells.warn: this repo's toolchain is defined by a devcontainer, but a hook runs on the HOST. Installs will use whatever host tooling exists, which may be the wrong version or absent entirely. Set `shell` by hand (for example to a `docker compose run --rm <service>` wrapper) if host installs are wrong.
shells.reason: a devcontainer describes a container the hook is not running inside, so there is no correct non-interactive wrapper to infer
no toolchain marker found, so commands run on the host shell as-is — which is correct for a repo whose tooling is simply installed globally

_comment: After proposing a shell, calibration runs ONE bounded version check per detected tool. Seconds,
no side effects, no database, no install. This catches the largest real class of 'the profile
looks right and is wrong': a wrong wrapper, or a toolchain absent from the host.
`versionArgs` is per tool because there is no universal spelling. `go --version` does not exist —
it exits non-zero with a usage error — so hard-coding `--version` would report 'toolchain absent'
for every healthy Go repo, which is precisely the false positive the probe exists to avoid.
Full prove-by-installing is deliberately NOT done here: it costs minutes, and an install that
TIMEOUT IS 180s because a COLD nix flake evaluation measured over 60s on a real repository,
which made an earlier 60s budget report a false 'the wrapper is wrong for this repo'. A timeout
is reported as INCONCLUSIVE, never as a failure — the two mean different things to a developer.

hazards.reason: composer runs these on every `composer install`, not just post-install-cmd. A framework repo conventionally hangs its migration off post-autoload-dump, so probing one key reported such a repo as clean — and bootstrapping a worktree would then migrate the SHARED development database that every other worktree and the main checkout also point at.
hazards.corroboration: CI is usually already guarding this; if the repo's workflows pass --no-scripts, say so — it is independent confirmation, not a guess.

hazards.reason: a postinstall that builds assets is real work a runnable worktree genuinely needs, so keep it — but it is usually the single largest part of bootstrap time, and the developer should know that is where the wait comes from.

bundler itself runs no post-install hook, but many Rails repos wrap `bundle install` in a setup task that also loads the schema. If the install command comes from such a task rather than from bundler directly, check what else it does.

_comment: MATCH THE WHOLE CHAIN, NOT THE FIRST LINK. The probe returns a script's immediate value, and in
real repos that value is almost always a reference to somewhere else. A real repository is the
worked example and it defeats a naive one-level match twice over:
post-install-cmd -> ["@db", ...]          the pattern sees only "@db"
@db              -> [..., "@db:migrate"]  one more hop to the match
@db:migrate      -> App\Composer\Scripts::dbMigrate   camelCase, hence caseInsensitive
So follow these forms until they bottom out, and match the pattern against every level.
A MATCH AND AN UNREADABLE TRAIL ARE DIFFERENT FINDINGS, reported under different labels.
Nearly every real composer post-install chain ends in a code callback, so treating every
unfollowable trail as 'a migration was found' would fire on almost every repository and the
alarm would stop meaning anything — the developer learns to click through it, which is worse
than not having it. A pattern match emits `escalate` (this WILL migrate; refuse and ask). An
unfollowable trail emits `unreadable` (this MIGHT; confirm). Both reach the developer; only one
claims to have found something.
forms: @name — another script in the same manifest
npm run <name> / pnpm run <name> / yarn <name> — another script in package.json
make <target> / just <recipe> — a Makefile or justfile target
bin/console <cmd>, php artisan <cmd>, rake <task>, mix <task> — a framework command
Fully\Qualified\Class::method — a code callback; read the method if it is in the repo
a path to a script file in the repo — read it
resolveIndirection.unresolvedReason: This install runs a script whose trail could not be followed to the end, so it is UNKNOWN rather than known-dangerous — do not present it as a migration that was found. Say which script it was and how far the trail went, and ask the developer to confirm it does not touch shared state. Most such chains end in ordinary cache or asset work and are fine; the point is that nobody can tell from the repository alone, and the cost of being wrong is a colleague's data.

escalations.reason: An install that migrates is the one failure mode with no recovery: it runs against the SHARED development database. Never neutralise this silently. State exactly which script was found and what it calls, then ASK — the developer may know it is safe, or may need a different command entirely.

_comment: Where this repo may have ALREADY answered the same question, in an artifact that has been
tested. Read these to CORROBORATE a proposal, and cite the file when you do — a hazard flag
backed by 'your own CI already passes --no-scripts' is far more convincing than a rule.
NEVER IMPORT THE FLAGS VERBATIM. CI optimises for a throwaway machine running one job; a
worktree is a development environment. Production flags (--no-dev, --omit=dev) would leave it
with no dev dependencies and so no test runner, and scoping flags (--filter) would install one
package of a workspace. It was checked against a real repository's CI.
Take the CORROBORATION, drop the flags.
STRIPPING IS NOT UNCONDITIONAL. A flag that SUPPRESSES SOMETHING DANGEROUS must be kept, not
stripped — see keepFlags.

keepFlags._comment: Safety flags. Finding one of these in CI is corroboration to KEEP it in the proposed command, never to remove it. `--ignore-scripts` and `--no-scripts` suppress arbitrary dependency- or repo-authored lifecycle code; that is exactly what a hook running unattended before the UI renders must not execute.

stripFlagsWithValue._comment: These take a value, so strip the flag AND its argument — and handle the `--flag=value` form too. NOTE `-w` is deliberately NOT here: for npm it is short for --workspace and takes a value, but for pnpm it is --workspace-root and is a BOOLEAN. Treating it as valued would swallow the next real flag, turning `pnpm install -w --frozen-lockfile` into `pnpm install` — a non-frozen install that can rewrite the lockfile. It is in stripFlags instead, which is safe for both.

neverFrom.shell: CI has no nix and no direnv — it installs the toolchain itself. A shell wrapper taken from CI would be wrong on a developer machine, and wrong in a way that only shows up as 'command not found' inside a hook.

_comment: Gitignored config a fresh checkout is missing and cannot regenerate. These become a proposed
.worktreeinclude, NOT profile `copy` entries — .worktreeinclude stays authoritative,
it is native behaviour that keeps working if this plugin is uninstalled, and repos already
using it get taken over transparently.
A candidate only counts if it is ACTUALLY GITIGNORED. Native .worktreeinclude copying applies
the gitignored-only rule, so listing a tracked file there does nothing, and listing a file
that does not exist is noise. Confirm with `git check-ignore` before proposing.

neverPropose._comment: Credentials, keys and machine state. Secrets belong in a copied .env, never in the committed profile — and several of these are actively harmful to duplicate: a second worktree writing a copied SQLite file or terraform state corrupts the original. Registry-credential files are here as a class: auth.json (composer), .npmrc (npm), .netrc, .git-credentials all carry tokens, so none of them is proposed.

_comment: WHERE TO LOOK FOR HINTS ONLY. Layer 3 is never inferred: nothing in a repo states
that an env var selects a tenant database. Everything found here is offered as a HINT next to
an AskUserQuestion, never as a pre-filled default, and 'no runtime isolation' is always an
offered outcome. A `runtime` block the developer did not explicitly confirm must not be written.
These are search locations and generic patterns, deliberately NOT rules that conclude anything —
and deliberately not any one project's variable names. A repo whose tenant selector is spelled
something this pattern misses is exactly why the developer is ASKED rather than told.
The tenancy family — INSTALLATION/TENANT/SITE/CLIENT/ORG/ACCOUNT/WORKSPACE/SCHEMA plus a suffix —
is there because a multi-tenant app's collidable state is usually keyed on one of them, and that is
a naming CONVENTION rather than any one project's variable. It is deliberately a family and not a
list of names seen in a particular repository: matching a convention keeps the engine general, while
matching a name would put one repo's identity into a table shipped to everyone.
And it is still only a HINT. A repo whose selector is spelled something this family misses is
precisely why the developer is asked rather than told — the pattern's job is to save typing, never
to reach a conclusion.
neverHintPattern drops credential-shaped variable NAMES from the hint list. Found by running this
against a real repository: the tenancy family matched ACCOUNTING_CREDENTIAL_KEY, and offering that
as a runtime candidate invites the one thing the profile forbids — a secret in a committed profile. The
name alone is not a leak, but a hint is a suggestion, and this is not a variable to suggest.
_comment_assignSources: Files where a repo's own COMMANDS are written down — agent guides, READMEs, task runners, manifests.
A `NAME=value command` prefix here, for a variable that is also a port or database hint, sets the
variable in the PROCESS environment, which beats every dotenv file — so a session following the repo's
own instructions inside a worktree would bypass the plugin's overrides and hit the shared state. Found
on a real repository whose every database command was documented with the tenant pinned inline.
Reported as `assign` records for the skill to raise; never acted on.
_comment_start: WHERE THE REPO WRITES DOWN HOW ITS APP STARTS, for `start` records. A port nothing reads isolates
nothing, so setup must find out how the dev server takes its port before it writes runtime.port:
a variable the app reads, a flag, or a compose mapping. These records save it the reading; they
decide nothing. startScriptNames are read from each startManifest's `scripts`; every `name: command`
line of a startProcfile is a process; a line of a startSource is reported when it matches
startCommandPattern (capped at startLinesPerFile per file). startPortPattern pulls the first port
literal or port flag out of each command, so a hardcoded port is visible at a glance. Generic
server invocations per ecosystem, never one project's command.
runtimeHints.startCommandPattern: (symfony (serve|server:start|local:server:start)|console server:(run|start)|rails (s|server)([[:space:]]|$)|manage\.py runserver|php -S |artisan serve|uvicorn |gunicorn |flask run|hypercorn |vite([[:space:]]+(dev|serve|preview|--)|[[:space:]]*$)|next (dev|start)|nuxt dev|astro dev|webpack serve|webpack-dev-server|ng serve|hugo server|phx\.server|puma |(npm|pnpm|yarn|bun) (run )?(dev|start|serve)([[:space:]]|$)|(docker compose|docker-compose) up)
_comment_pluginPaths: Paths the plugin itself may create INSIDE a checkout. Each must be gitignored: an untracked file
there is work to the teardown guard, so the worktree would never be torn down, and a
committed opt-out marker would switch layer 3 off for the whole team. Reported as `ignore` records.

_comment_chainMaxDepth: How many hops of script indirection to follow before giving up. Top-level ON PURPOSE: it used to
live at escalations[0].resolveIndirection.maxDepth, which the plugin's JSON layer cannot address
because it cannot index into an array — so it read as empty and the hardcoded fallback always won,
meaning tuning it here changed nothing. Running out of budget now counts as an unfollowable trail
and escalates, rather than being reported as a fully-followed clean chain.
_comment_unresolvedLeafPattern: A chain leaf matching this is a trail detection cannot follow — a code callback, a script file.
Top-level for the same reason as chainMaxDepth: it briefly lived inside escalations[0], an ARRAY
element, which the dotted-path JSON layer cannot address. It read as empty and the hardcoded
fallback in detect.sh always won, so editing it here changed nothing and the two copies could
diverge silently. Anything tunable must live where the reader can actually reach it.
